This notebook is setting up the environment for the DHS Nepal
Prospector. It interactively builds each of the components
for the prospector using Quarto notebooks connected to
a bare bones iPython kernel with Singularity loaded.

```{python}
from pathlib import Path
from pyprojroot import here
import os
from spython.main import Client
import subprocess
from rich.console import Console
from rich.panel import Panel

console = Console()

user = os.environ["USER"]

project = here(
    "/n/holylabs/cgolden_lab/Lab/frontier/works/prospectors/prospectorDHSNepal"
)

sandbox_root = project / "sandbox"

sandbox = sandbox_root / f"{user}-prospectorDHSNepal-sandbox"

sif = project / ".devcontainer" / "prospector-dhsnepal-amd64.sif"

# Keep temporary build/cache material on node-local /tmp.
# Do not put durable containers or project state here.
os.environ["TMPDIR"] = "/tmp"
os.environ["SINGULARITY_TMPDIR"] = "/tmp"
os.environ["SINGULARITY_CACHEDIR"] = f"/tmp/{user}-singularity-cache"

Path(os.environ["SINGULARITY_CACHEDIR"]).mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
sandbox_root.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

console.print(
    Panel.fit(
        f"Project: {project}\n"
        f"SIF: {sif}\n"
        f"Sandbox: {sandbox}\n"
        f"Singularity cache: {os.environ['SINGULARITY_CACHEDIR']}",
        title="Prospector DHS Nepal Runtime",
    )
)
```

This is the target image.

We'll be using the `spython` library to build and
run the image. The `Client` class provides a simple
interface for interacting with Singularity images. We'll
start with a Spack base:

```{python}
base_image = "docker://spack/rockylinux8:develop"
```

```{python}
Client.build(
    image=str(sandbox),
    recipe="docker://spack/rockylinux8:develop",
    options=[
        "--fakeroot", "--sandbox",
        "--fix-perms", "--force"
        ],
    sudo=False,
)
```

Nice! We can see that the actual file is a sandbox directory. Now,
let's add the `/work` dir:

```{python}
res = Client.execute(
    image=str(sandbox),
    command=[
        "bash", "-lc",
        "mkdir", "-p", "/work"],
    options=["--fakeroot", "--writable"],
    sudo=False,
)

res
```


::: {.callout-tip}
Why add `bash -lc`? It's necessary because when the Client runs
an exec call, it doesn't start a shell, which means all of the
variables and executables aren't necessarily discoverable, even
if they are installed.
:::


At this point, we can define some
helpful functions to make it easier to iterate:

```{python}
def run(cmd, bind_project=False, sandbox=sandbox):

    options = ["--fakeroot", "--writable", "--no-home"]
    if bind_project:
        options += ["--bind", f"{project}:/work"]

    final_command = [
        "singularity",
        "exec",
        *options,
        str(sandbox),
        "bash", "--noprofile", "--norc", "-c", cmd
    ]

    result = subprocess.run(
        final_command,
        capture_output=True,
        text=True,
    )
    return result
```

```{python}
from subprocess import CompletedProcess
from rich.console import Console
from rich.panel import Panel
from rich.text import Text
from rich.columns import Columns

console = Console()

def show(result):

    stdout = Panel(
        result.stdout.rstrip() or "<empty>",
        title="stdout",
        border_style="green",
    )

    stderr = Panel(
        result.stderr.rstrip() or "<empty>",
        title="stderr",
        border_style="yellow",
    )

    console.print(
        Panel(
            Columns([stdout, stderr]),
            title=f"Exit code: {result.returncode}",
            subtitle=" ".join(result.args),
            border_style="green" if result.returncode == 0 else "red",
        )
    )
```

```{python}
show(run("ls /"))
```

Next, we know that `spack` is in the container but
we need to run it explicitly. I think this is how:

```{python}
show(run(". /opt/spack/share/spack/setup-env.sh && spack --version"))
```

Great! Next, we'll install all of the expected dependencies
for the prospector. To do this, we'll bind mount the
actual project directory to the container and run spack
install commands. This will ensure that the container has
all of the necessary dependencies, because we've created the
spack YAML file ahead of time for the prospector to run.

```{python}
show(run("ls /work", bind_project=False))
```

```{python}
show(run("mkdir -p /work && cd /work", bind_project=False))
```

```{python}
show(run("ls /work", bind_project=True))
```

What this shows is that the process of building a container this
way is quite literal and sequential. If you do `mkdir`, the changes
persist even in this notebook interface. We are, therefore,
able to build the container in a stepwise manner, which is nice for
debugging.

```{python}
show(run("pwd", bind_project=True))
```

Entering the exact path is still required, though!

## Basic Setup

The base layer is where we will install linux system level dependencies.
This is done with `dnf`, since we're using Rocky Linux 8 as the
base image. To get this information, we'll check the output
of `pak::pkg_sysreqs`. We use the rproject.toml file to populate
the list of system dependencies. The following was run
in a terminal:

```r
pkgs <- toml::read_toml("rproject.toml")$project$dependencies
pkgs[[22]] <- NULL # remove the sess package; it's not ready yet
pak::pkg_sysreqs(unlist(pkgs), sysreqs_platform = "rockylinux")
```

The following command will install the necessary
packages for the prospector to run.

```{python}

```

Note that the below doesn't work with newlines and `\` line breaks, so
we have to run it as a single line. This is a bit annoying, but it
works. The `dnf` command is installing all of the system dependencies
for the prospector to run. This is a one-time setup step, and it will
take a few minutes to complete. Once it's done, we can move on to the
next step of building the prospector.

```{python}
show(run("""
dnf install -y cmake make libcurl-devel openssl-devel git libX11-devel abseil-cpp-devel udunits2-devel libxml2-devel libicu-devel fontconfig-devel freetype-devel cairo-devel libpng-devel libtiff-devel sqlite-devel fribidi-devel harfbuzz-devel
"""))
```

Great! Next, we get spack to install the project's dependencies.

## Project Dependencies

To get the Spack dependencies ready, we run spack concretize. This will read the `spack.yaml` file
and generate a concrete spec for the environment. This is a one-time setup step, and it will take
a few minutes to complete. Once it's done, we can move on to the next step of building the
prospector.

```{python}
show(run("""
. /opt/spack/share/spack/setup-env.sh && cd /work && spack env activate -d . && spack concretize
""", bind_project=True))
```

The above takes very little time, but below takes a while:

```{python}
#| eval: false
# show(run("""
# . /opt/spack/share/spack/setup-env.sh && cd /work && spack env activate -d . && spack install
# """, bind_project=True))
```

We're actually not going to run the above interactively, as it
always times out. Instead, we'll learn how to run it as a SLURM
job right from here in the notebook using `subprocess` and `submitit`,
The following is a simple example of how to run a slurm job from a
notebook using `submitit`. The `submitit` library provides a simple
interface for submitting jobs to a SLURM cluster. We'll use it to submit
the spack install command as a job. First, an example:

```{python}
import submitit

def add(x, y):
    return x + y
```

The `AutoExecutor` class is the interface for submitting function to a cluster or run them locally.
The specified folder is used to dump job information, logs and result when finished; `%j` is replaced by the job id at runtime.

```{python}
log_folder = here() / "notebooks" / "prospector_dhsnepal" / "log_test/%j"
executor = submitit.AutoExecutor(folder=log_folder)
```

The AutoExecutor provides a simple abstraction over SLURM to simplify 
switching between local and SLURM jobs (or other clusters if plugins 
are available). 

You can specify `sbatch` parameters right inside Python (below it 
will timeout after 4min, and run on `hsph`). This is where you 
would specify `gpus_per_node=1` for instance.

Cluster specific options must be appended by the cluster name, e.g.
SLURM partition can be specified using `slurm_partition` argument. It
will be ignored on other clusters:

```{python}
executor.update_parameters(
    timeout_min=4, 
    slurm_partition="hsph",
    mem_gb=1.0,
    cpus_per_task=1
    )
```

The submission interface is identical to `concurrent.futures.Executor`

```{python}
job = executor.submit(add, 5, 7)  # will compute add(5, 7)
print(job.job_id)  # ID of your job
```

After some time, it will complete and we can retrieve the
result; this is a blocking call, so it will wait until the job is 
finished. If the job failed, it will raise an error with the 
corresponding trace.:

```{python}
output = job.result()  # waits for the submitted function to complete and returns its output
```

if ever the job failed, job.result() will raise an error with the corresponding trace

```{python}
assert output == 12  # 5 + 7 = 12...  your addition was computed in the cluster and returned to you
```

Note that this returned a Python Object!! This is because
under the hood, `submitit` is using `cloudpickle` to 
serialize the function and its arguments, send it to the 
cluster, and then deserialize the result back to Python. 
This is a powerful feature that allows you to run arbitrary 
Python code on a cluster without having to worry about the 
details of job submission and management.

With that in mind, we can now submit the spack install 
command as a job. All we have to do is decorate our run script
with the `submitit` executor:


```{python}
def submit_run(*args, **kwargs):
    return executor.submit(run, *args, **kwargs)
```

With this decorator, we now have a scenario where every time
we call `submit_run` with arguments, it will run `executor.submit(run, *args, **kwargs)` 
and return a `submitit.Job` object. This is a powerful feature that 
allows us to run arbitrary Python code on a cluster without having to 
worry about the details of job submission and management.

For example, with a test:

```{python}
job=submit_run("ls /work", bind_project=True)
```

Now, define an executor beefy enough to handle this.
I think we should submit something that takes at least
6 hours, and we should request 8 CPUs and 32 GB of RAM.


```{python}
n_cpus = 8
executor.update_parameters(
    timeout_min=360, 
    slurm_partition="hsph",
    mem_gb=32.0,
    cpus_per_task=n_cpus
    )
```

And now, submit:

```{python}
job=submit_run(
    f". /opt/spack/share/spack/setup-env.sh && cd /work && spack env activate -d . && spack install --fail-fast -j{n_cpus}", 
    bind_project=True
)
```

The job_id for now is: `24981908`

```{python}
job.job_id
```
